title: Perceptions and preparedness of K-12 educators in adopting generative AI
extended_summary:
This paper examines how K-12 educators perceive generative AI and how prepared they feel to adopt it in school settings. The study addresses a practical problem in education: AI tools such as ChatGPT and DALL-E are becoming more visible, but schools vary widely in readiness, policy support, and teacher confidence. The author focuses on educators’ familiarity with AI, their perceptions of its benefits and risks, and the institutional conditions that shape adoption.

The study uses a mixed-methods survey design with 250 K-12 educators from rural, suburban, and urban schools across public, charter, and private institutions in the United States. Participants included teachers, principals, vice principals, superintendents, and instructional coaches. Quantitative survey items measured AI familiarity, perceived impact, and institutional planning stage, while open-ended responses were thematically analyzed to identify common concerns and opportunities. Data collection occurred online over 2024, and the survey was anonymous and IRB-approved.

Findings suggest that educators generally view generative AI positively, especially for operational efficiency, lesson planning, personalized learning, and student engagement. However, readiness is uneven: leaders reported higher preparedness than teachers, and many respondents cited insufficient professional development, funding constraints, infrastructure gaps, and ethical concerns such as data privacy and algorithmic bias. The paper concludes that effective AI integration in K-12 education requires targeted training, strong leadership support, equitable access to resources, and clear institutional policies governing responsible use.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: Generative AI tools and chatbots used for producing text, images, lesson materials, and other educational outputs in K-12 settings; includes systems such as ChatGPT and DALL-E when discussed generally rather than as evaluated products.
identified_tools.use_case: Surveyed K-12 educators’ perceptions, familiarity, preparedness, and institutional readiness for adopting generative AI in teaching, lesson planning, administrative work, and broader school integration. The paper also discussed potential classroom uses and policy/implementation considerations, but did not evaluate a specific deployed tool in a school coaching system.

findings.finding_summary: In this mixed-methods survey of 250 K-12 educators, institutional readiness for AI integration varied substantially: 25% reported pilot programmes in progress or completed, 15% reported being fully invested and successfully deployed, and 20% were in short-term planning. The study also found a significant positive association between AI familiarity and perceived readiness (r = 0.45, p < 0.05), and regression results indicated that AI familiarity and institutional planning stage significantly predicted AI adoption (R² = 0.35).
findings.measure: Institutional planning stage, AI familiarity, perceived readiness, and AI adoption
findings.effect_size: r = 0.45; R² = 0.35; B = 0.40 (AI familiarity), B = 0.30 (institutional planning stage)

findings.finding_summary: Educators reported that generative AI was viewed positively for streamlining administrative and instructional preparation tasks, especially grading, lesson planning, and data analysis. The mean perception of AI’s impact was 4.1/5, with 40% rating it as extremely positive and 35% somewhat positive.
findings.measure: Perceptions of AI’s impact on efficiency and teaching work

findings.finding_summary: Participants described generative AI as useful for personalised learning and differentiated instruction, noting its ability to tailor lessons to student needs and support more advanced learners. However, the study also reported substantial concerns about lack of funding, infrastructure gaps, teacher preparedness, data privacy, algorithmic bias, and plagiarism, indicating that benefits were viewed alongside significant implementation barriers.
findings.measure: Qualitative thematic responses on personalised learning, differentiation, and implementation challenges

quality_tier_rationale: This is a mixed-methods survey study with descriptive statistics, correlations, and regression, not an experimental evaluation. The evidence is useful for implementation context but remains observational and self-reported.
impact_tier_rationale: Reported effects are modest to moderate in readiness/adoption associations (e.g., r = 0.45), but the paper does not test learning outcomes or a deployed intervention. The main contribution is implementation insight rather than demonstrated student impact.
